id: qml-06
title: Power of data
paper: Huang et al., Power of data in quantum machine learning (arXiv Nov 2020; Nature Communications 12, 2631, 2021)
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01938
type: Mechanism
cutoff: 2020-11-03
domain: qml
profile: advantage

## expected_verdict
Supported (scoped). Two halves must both survive. The negative half: data lifts classical models, so standard quantum kernels lose on real-like data. The positive half: projected quantum kernels win by >20% on data engineered to maximize geometric difference. Usefulness on natural data stays open.

## I0
When does geometric difference permit a projected quantum kernel to improve prediction?

## evidence
- Prediction-error bound s_K(N)/N; geometric difference g(K_C‖K_Q) bounds when a classical kernel can match a quantum one (s_C ≤ g² s_Q); effective dimension d of the quantum feature space.
- Theory: with N ∝ p²/ε² data, classical ML can predict some classically hard-to-compute quantum functions ("power of data").
- Projected quantum kernel: Gaussian kernel on 1-RDMs of the embedded state.
- Data: fashion-MNIST (shirts vs dresses), PCA to n dims; embeddings E1 separable, E2 IQP, E3 Hamiltonian evolution; quantum labels from a local observable after a random-coupling Heisenberg QNN; up to 30 qubits in simulation (~1.1 petaflop/s peak).
- Fig. 3: on classical data, classical ML is best; on quantum-labelled data, tuned classical models are "very competitive and can even outperform existing quantum ML models".
- Fig. 4: engineered labels with s_PQ = 1, s_C = g²; PQ advantage tracks g and exceeds 20% at large sizes for E3; baselines: best of Gaussian SVM, linear SVM, AdaBoost, random forest, neural nets, gradient boosting (tuned).
- Authors: advantage diminishes as N grows; "true advantage" claims also need classical approximations of quantum models.

## intake
- Scope: (A) a test for potential advantage via g and d; (B) projected quantum kernels outperform tuned classical models on labels engineered to saturate s_C = g² s_PQ.
- Regime: simulated noiseless circuits up to 30 qubits; fixed training-set size; fashion-MNIST-derived inputs.
- Assumptions: labels are generated by (or engineered against) the quantum embedding; classical models get the raw input, not the embedding; kernel methods bound the classical comparators.
- Falsifiers: a classical approximation of the 1-RDM features (e.g. via simulation or shadows) matches PQ; the gap closes on non-engineered labels or with more data N.

## screen
- Must flag: the positive result is on engineered labels; the classical comparator set is restricted to standard models; advantage shrinks with N.
- Must request: results on natural labels; classical surrogates of the projected features.

## retrieval
- Pre-cutoff must-finds: Havlíček et al. 2018 and Schuld & Killoran quantum kernels; classical shadows (Huang, Kueng, Preskill 2020); Liu, Arunachalam & Temme 2020 rigorous speed-up.
- Current-mode critique: Bowles, Ahmed & Schuld 2024: ProjectedQuantumKernel included; classical baselines outperform overall; in higher dimensions its Gram matrix resembles the classical SVC, raising whether the Gaussian post-processing does the learning.

## designer
- Arms: PQ kernel, standard quantum kernel, tuned classical models; datasets with low and high g, engineered and natural labels; vary N.
- Pre-register: compute g before seeing labels; success = PQ beats the best tuned classical model on non-engineered labels.

## champion
- Best of tuned Gaussian SVM, gradient boosting, random forest, MLP (as in the paper), plus a classical surrogate of the projected features where simulable.

## panel
- Flaw: the headline "significant prediction advantage" is on data built to produce it. Repair: report it as an existence demonstration; keep the negative (power-of-data) result as the main practical message.

## run
- Recompute at small n (≤ 12 qubits): g(K_C‖K_Q) and g(K_C‖K_PQ) for E1–E3 on fashion-MNIST PCA; reproduce the trend that g grows E1 → E3 and PQ accuracy tracks g. Code via TensorFlow Quantum; 30-qubit runs are out of local scope.

## verdict
- Label: Supported (scoped): prediction advantage exists on engineered datasets at up to 30 simulated qubits; classical models with data are competitive on the other tasks.
- Must say: engineered labels; natural-data advantage not shown; Bowles et al. find classical models ahead on their benchmarks.
- Must not say: a practical quantum learning advantage on real data; or the result is refuted (the benchmark tested different datasets).

## audit
- Check: 30 qubits; >20% advantage (Fig. 4); classical model list; s_PQ = 1 construction (Appendix G); statement that advantage diminishes with N.

## variants
- Natural quantum datasets (e.g. phases of matter) with g computed in advance; or classical shadow surrogates for 1-RDM features. Cheapest: compute g on a public quantum dataset before training.
